Abstract
Objective  This study aimed to identify the hyoid bone (HB) using the nnU-Net based artificial intelligence (AI) model 
in cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) images and assess the model’s success in automatic segmentation.
Methods  CBCT images of 190 patients were randomly selected. The raw data was converted to DICOM format and 
transferred to the 3D Slicer Imaging Software (Version 4.10.2; MIT, Cambridge, MA, USA). HB was labeled manually 
using the 3D Slicer. The dataset was divided into training, validation, and test sets in a ratio of 8:1:1. The nnU-Net 
v2 architecture was utilized to process the training and test datasets, generating the algorithm weight factors. To 
assess the model’s accuracy and performance, a confusion matrix was employed. F1-score, Dice coefficient (DC), 95% 
Hausdorff distance (95% HD), and Intersection over Union (IoU) metrics were calculated to evaluate the results.
Results  The model’s performance metrics were as follows: DC = 0.9434, IoU = 0.8941, F1-score = 0.9446, and 95% 
HD = 1.9998. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was generated, yielding an AUC value of 0.98.
Conclusion  The results indicated that the nnU-Net v2 model achieved high precision and accuracy in HB 
segmentation on CBCT images. Automatic segmentation of HB can enhance clinicians’ decision-making speed and 
accuracy in diagnosing and treating various clinical conditions.
Clinical trial number  Not applicable.

Introduction
The hyoid bone (HB) is a U-shaped, mobile bone located 
at the level of the third cervical vertebra, positioned 
between the mandible and thyroid cartilage. This bone 
forms the movable base of the tongue, provides connec­
tion foci for the middle part of the pharynx and main­
tains the pharynx opening, which is necessary during 
swallowing and respiratory functions. Due to its anatom­
ical location and relationship with cervicofacial struc­
tures, the clinical significance of the HB in orthodontics 
and dentofacial orthopedics has grown. Additionally, in 
surgical procedures (e.g., thyroidectomy, neck dissec­
tions), understanding the anatomical relationships of the 
hyoid bone is important for preventing complications 
[1–4]. Studies have shown that the HB’s position may 
vary based on the mandibular bone and facial structure. 
Additionally, the HB adapts to anteroposterior changes 
in head position [5–7]. Research indicates that alterations 
in HB position can influence the temporomandibular 
joint (TMJ), potentially causing TMJ disorders [8]. For 
instance, Ekici et al. [9] found a correlation between TMJ 
disease and HB position using lateral cephalometric radi­
ography, noting that the hyoid angle was larger in TMJ 
patients than in the control group.
In forensic medicine, examining the HB is crucial for 
accurate diagnostic evaluations. Fractures of the HB can 
indicate cervical compression, perimortem drowning, or 
trauma [10]. Additionally, age and gender estimation can 
be determined by measuring the HB’s anatomical dimen­
sions, volume, and the distance between the corpus and 
the greater horn. This information can assist in orthodon­
tic treatment planning [11, 12]. The HB can be evaluated 
using various imaging methods such as ultrasonography 
(USG) [13], computed tomography (CT) [14], cone beam 
computed tomography (CBCT) [15], lateral cephalomet­
ric radiography [15], and panoramic radiographs [16].
The integration of artificial intelligence in medical 
imaging has significantly advanced the field of diagnostic 
radiology, particularly in automating complex tasks such 
as lesion and anatomical structure segmentation. For 
example, Comelli et al. [17] developed a smart,operator-
independent system for delineating tumors in positron 
emission tomography (PET) scans, demonstrating the 
feasibility and reliability of deep learning approaches in 
producing consistent and reproducible results without 
manual intervention. Their findings highlight how AI can 
streamline clinical workflows, reduce observer variability, 
and enhance diagnostic accuracy.
In the domain of dental and orthopedic imaging, the 
application of deep learning to CBCT data has gained 
momentum due to the growing need for precise and 
efficient 3D modeling. A recent study by Tiribilli et al. 
[18] demonstrated a contemporary deep learning-based 
workflow utilizing the nnU-Net framework for automatic 
bone segmentation and 3D reconstruction in CBCT 
orthopedic imaging. Their results confirmed the adapt­
ability and robustness of nnU-Net in handling complex 
anatomical variations while producing clinically viable 
models. This work underscores the potential of nnU-Net 
not only in traditional medical imaging but also in den­
tal applications, where detailed anatomical modeling is 
essential. Inspired by this advancement, our study applies 
the nnU-Net v2 architecture for the segmentation of the 
hyoid bone in CBCT scans, contributing further evidence 
of the framework’s applicability in head and neck imaging 
tasks.
A previous study has explored the automatic segmen­
tation of the HB using artificial intelligence (AI) on fluo­
roscopy images [19]. However, there have been no studies 
on automatic segmentation of the HB on CBCT images. 
This study aims to perform automatic segmentation of 
the HB on CBCT images using the nnU-Net v2 convo­
lutional neural networks (CNNs). This model stream­
lines the system through a systematic approach without 
adding new network structures and can be transformed 
into a semi-automatic system with manual additions to 
enhance performance [20].
Manual labeling of CBCT scans is tedious, time-con­
suming, and expensive. Semi-automatic labeling still 
requires operator involvement, leading to potential mis­
takes. Therefore, fully automatic labeling in CBCT scans 
is needed [21–24]. This study evaluates the success of the 
nnU-Net v2 model for HB in clinical research environ­
ments and its potential applications in determining HB 
position in individuals with different skeletal closures and 
patients with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS). 
Additionally, it may provide practical information in 
forensic medicine and dentistry about changes in the HB 
due to neck trauma. The study hypothesizes that AI can 
identify HB from CBCT images at least as well as experts.
Materials and methods
Study design and ethical approval
This study utilized CBCT images from patients referred 
to Inonu University, Faculty of Dentistry - Dentomaxil­
lofacial Radiology Unit. Its objective was to design and 
validate an AI-based method for automatic HB segmen­
tation, consisting of three phases: development, training, 
and testing. 3D images were processed using the nnU-
Net v2 convolutional neural network algorithm for 3D 
automated HB detection, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The study 
followed the CLAIM and STARD guidelines for article 
preparation. This retrospective study complied with the 
Helsinki Declaration and other comparable ethical guide­
lines, with approval from the Research Ethics Committee 
of Inonu University (decision no: 2025/6807). Written 
consent for scientific research usage was obtained from 
individuals.

Sample size and inclusion criteria
The sample size of this study was calculated using 
G*Power software (v3.1.9.7). A power analysis was per­
formed for a paired two-sample t-test, assuming a sta­
tistical power of 95% (1-β = 0.95), a significance level of 
5% (α = 0.05), and an effect size of dz = 0.263. Although 
the paired t-test is traditionally used for before-after 
comparisons, it was employed here to estimate the mini­
mum sample size required for statistically meaningful 
comparisons between manual and automated segmenta­
tion performance in future evaluation steps. This analy­
sis determined that at least 190 cases were sufficient to 
ensure robust model training and evaluation.
Accordingly, 190 cone-beam computed tomography 
(CBCT) images (100 male and 90 female) of individuals 
aged 20–62 years (mean age: 41 years) were retrospec­
tively evaluated. The following inclusion and exclusion 
criteria were applied:
Inclusion criteria:
 	•
Individuals aged 18 years or older.
 	•
Individuals without syndromes or bone diseases.
 	•
CBCT images with clearly identified HB margins.
Exclusion criteria:
 	•
CBCT images with styloid process fused with HB.
 	•
Individuals with neck and cervical region surgeries 
or trauma.
 	•
CBCT images exhibiting motion or metal artifacts 
that compromise diagnostic accuracy.
CBCT data acquisition and analysis
The scans were conducted utilizing a NewTom 5G CBCT 
machine (QR of Verona, Italy) with parameters: 110 
kVp, 1–20 mA, 3.6 s, and 18 × 16 cm FOV with 0.3 mm 
voxel size. CBCT images were acquired between 2022 
and 2024. All scans were performed with the patients 
in a standardized upright position to ensure consistency 
in head orientation and anatomical alignment. Radio­
graphic protocols were designed to comply with ALARA 
(As Low As Reasonably Achievable) principles, mini­
mizing radiation exposure while preserving diagnostic 
quality.
The datasets included a diverse patient population with 
varying anatomical structures and skeletal classifica­
tions, enhancing the model’s ability to generalize across 
different clinical cases. Prior to model training, all scans 
were anonymized in accordance with data protection 
regulations and reviewed by experienced radiologists to 
confirm the presence and visibility of the HB. Image pre­
processing steps included resampling to a uniform voxel 
resolution and standardizing image intensity values. This 
ensured compatibility across scans and optimized input 
consistency for the deep learning model. These prepara­
tory steps laid the foundation for accurate segmentation 
and reliable model performance across all subsets of the 
data.

Ground truth
CBCT images were imported into 3D Slicer (Version 
4.10.2; MIT, Cambridge, MA, USA) for manual labeling 
of the hyoid bone in coronal, sagittal, and axial planes 
(Fig. 2). 3D Slicer, as a powerful tool for medical image 
processing and analysis, allows for precise segmentation 
in different planes. The segmented DICOM data were 
converted into NIfTI format for further processing, mak­
ing the data suitable for advanced analysis. This format 
conversion ensures segmentation with high resolution 
and without data loss.
The segmentation process was manually carried out 
by two experienced dentomaxillofacial radiologists (E.H. 
and I.G.), and they reached a consensus on the ground 
truth. This ensured that both radiologists’ decisions and 
labeling during the segmentation process were aligned. 
The segmentation was carefully performed to ensure high 
accuracy and consistency. Additionally, the segmentation 
results were reviewed and fully agreed upon by senior 
maxillofacial radiologists (S.B.D. and F.K.). This valida­
tion process is critical to assess how well the model aligns 
with real-world data.
Testing data
To evaluate model performance and reduce overfitting, 
10-fold cross-validation was performed on a training 
dataset (n = 171). For each fold, the model was trained 
on 90% of the data and validated on the remaining 10%. 
The hyperparameters yielding optimal performance were 
determined through this iterative process. After cross-
validation, the final model was retrained from scratch 
using the entire training set (n = 171) and tested on an 
independent hold-out test set (n = 19) (Fig.  3). Train­
ing involved a CNN model based on nnU-Net v2, 1000 
epochs, learning rate 0.00001, using Python v3.6.1 and 
PyTorch library (Fig. 4). The CranioCatch AI Tool (Ver­
sion 2.1., CranioCatch, Eskisehir, Turkey) facilitated 
model development and training [25]. During training, 
key hyperparameters such as batch size, patch size, and 
optimizer settings were systematically fine-tuned based 
on preliminary validation results to maximize segmen­
tation accuracy while minimizing computational cost. 
Model training was performed using an NVIDIA Tesla 
V100 GPU with 16 GB VRAM, integrated within a Dell 
PowerEdge T640 GPU Calculation Server (Dell Inc., 
Round Rock, TX, USA). Mathematical processing and 
computational tasks were supported by the Dell Power­
Edge T640 Calculation Server and the Dell PowerEdge 
R540 Storage Server, all housed within the Dental-AI 
Laboratory at Eskisehir Osmangazi University Faculty 
of Dentistry. The average epoch time for the training 
process was 75.71 s. The nnU-Net v2 model was imple­
mented in Python and PyTorch, with additional software

dependencies including SimpleITK, nibabel, pydicom,

To ensure reproducibility, all random seeds were fixed, 
and detailed logging of training metrics and loss curves 
was performed throughout the entire process. Model 
performance was continuously monitored at each fold 
of cross-validation using standard evaluation metrics, 
including Dice Coefficient (DC), Intersection over Union 
(IoU), Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and Hausdorff Dis­
tance (HD). These metrics were visualized and compared 
across folds to evaluate consistency and overall model 
robustness.
Furthermore, early stopping criteria and learning rate 
schedulers were implemented to prevent overfitting 
and to dynamically adjust the training process based on 
trends in the validation loss. Model checkpoints were 
saved periodically, and the final model was selected by 
averaging the performance results from all cross-valida­
tion folds. In the post-training phase, the model’s gener­
alization ability was assessed on an independent test set 
(n = 19), where it continued to demonstrate high segmen­
tation performance, underscoring its potential utility in 
clinical applications. The integration of the CranioCatch 
AI Tool streamlined the entire workflow-from image 
preprocessing and annotation management to model 
training and evaluation-making it a practical solution for 
future use in dental and medical fields.
U-Net is a convolutional neural network architecture 
introduced in 2015, designed for biomedical image seg­
mentation. Its key innovation is the use of skip connec­
tions, which preserve fine details by linking encoder and 
decoder layers. nnU-Net, an advanced version, automati­
cally adapts hyperparameters and preprocessing for dif­
ferent datasets, reducing manual effort. While initially 
developed for medical imaging, U-Net is also used in 
satellite imagery, autonomous driving, and remote sens­
ing. Both 2D and 3D U-Net variants exist. In this study, 
we used the 3D variant, which is particularly effective for 
MRI and CT scans. The model performs well even with 
limited data thanks to data augmentation techniques 
like rotation and scaling. Additionally, specialized loss 
functions improve segmentation accuracy, especially on 
imbalanced datasets [26].
Evaluation
Model performance in automated 3D HB segmenta­
tion on CBCT volumes was evaluated using a confusion 
matrix, measuring algorithm accuracy with true positive

Results
The nnU-Net v2 model was used for HB segmentation on 
190 CBCT images, divided into training (n = 152), valida­
tion (n = 19), and test sets (n = 19). Training involved 1000 
epochs using the “Adam” optimization algorithm and 
ReLU activation (Table 1).
The performance evaluation of the model in automated 
hyoid bone segmentation shows high success in classi­
fication and segmentation tasks. The model’s precision 
value is 0.9309 and recall value is 0.9587, indicating that 
true positive examples are detected with high accuracy. 
In terms of segmentation success, high scores such as 
a DC of 0.9439 and IoU value of 0.8941 were obtained. 
An F1-Score of 0.9446 demonstrates that the model 
effectively balances precision and recall. Furthermore, 
the 95% Hausdorff Distance (95% HD) value of 1.9998 
shows that the predicted boundaries align closely with 
the actual anatomical boundaries. These comprehensive 
performance results prove that the nnU-Net v2 model, in 
terms of segmenting the hyoid bone, is a reliable, effec­
tive, and stable artificial intelligence tool that can be used 
in clinical applications (Table 2). The value of the metric 
values of the study is shown in Fig. 5.
The ROC curve is obtained by graphing the true posi­
tive and false positive rates, which can be used to reflect 
the relationship between sensitivity and specificity. The 
AUC value indicates the area under the ROC curve 
enclosed by the coordinate axes. The larger the AUC 
value, the better the effect of the machine learning model, 
and the higher its discriminative ability. The ROC curve 
yielded an AUC value of 0.98 (Fig. 6). The loss function 
measures the distance between the actual and predicted 
values of the target. Based on the measured value, it is 
concluded how close the model is to the desired value. A 
graph of dice scores and loss function values was created 
for each cycle from the model’s inception (Fig. 7).

Discussion
To our knowledge, no previous studies have explored 
HB segmentation using AI on CBCT images. This study 
aimed to evaluate the efficacy of the nnU-Net v2 model 
in segmenting HB using CBCT scans. The results were 
promising, with a Dice Coefficient (DC) of 0.9439, indi­
cating highly accurate HB segmentation. An Intersection 
over Union (IoU) metric above 0.5 is generally consid­
ered successful, and this study achieved an IoU of 0.8941 
for HB segmentation [27]. Furthermore, the F1-Score 
of 0.9446 suggests high sensitivity and precision. The 
Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve yielded 
an Area Under the Curve (AUC) value of 0.98, thus con­
firming the hypothesis (H1) that AI can accurately seg­
ment HB from CBCT images.
The HB is unique as it does not articulate with other 
bones in the head and neck region but is associated with 
many muscle groups [6]. Its position is influenced by 
functional and physical conditions in the head and neck 
region. Automatic segmentation of the HB can provide 
clinicians with insights into the position and angle of the 
hyoid in patients with different skeletal malocclusions. 
Previous studies observed significant changes in HB 
position following activator treatment for Class II mal­
occlusion and bimaxillary surgery for Class III malocclu­
sion [28, 29]. The nnU-Net v2 architecture can evaluate 
changes in HB position after orthognathic surgery and 
functional orthodontic treatment.
For patients with obstructive sleep apnea, treatment 
plans and preliminary screenings can consider the dis­
tance between the mandibular plane and the HB [30]. 
Significant changes in HB position have been observed 
in patients treated for myofascial pain [31]. Automated 
segmentation with the nnU-Net model could assess 
treatment effectiveness for obstructive sleep apnea and 
myofascial pain in the future. The distance between the 
cervical vertebra-HB and HB-mandible can predict diffi­
cult airway intubation in surgical cases [32–34]. AI-based 
for radiographic prediction of difficult intubation may be 
practical in clinical settings.
The maxillofacial region, affected by cysts, tumors, 
trauma, and congenital malformations, often requires dif­
ferent surgical treatments [35]. Previous studies have seg­
mented maxillofacial bones using AI, making this study 
innovative by performing 3D automatic segmentation of 
the HB in CBCT images [35–38]. Perimortem HB frac­
tures are crucial in forensic medicine, as they can indi­
cate blunt impact trauma or hanging [39]. The presented 
deep learning algorithm successfully segmented the HB, 
aiding the evaluation of HB anatomy and facilitating the

In some cases, the stylohyoid ligament extends exces­
sively and fuses with the hyoid bone, leading to Hyoid 
Syndrome. Patients experience pain during functional 
movements such as chewing and swallowing, which may 
intensify with mandibular or neck movement. Hyoid 
Syndrome and Eagle Syndrome can co-occur [1, 40, 41]. 
HB segmentation on CBCT scans may aid in diagnosing 
Hyoid Syndrome in patients with clinical complaints.
Several studies utilizing the U-Net model success­
fully performed automatic segmentation of the maxil­
lary sinus [27], facial bones [35] and bony part of the 
temporomandibular joint in 3D images. For the maxil­
lary sinus, IoU and F1-score were reported as 0.9275 
and 0.9784, respectively [27]. For facial bones, the aver­
age DC was 0.897 [35]. Vinayahalingam et al. [38] evalu­
ated AI performance in CBCT-based segmentation of the 
mandibular condyle and glenoid fossa, reporting DC and 
IoU scores of 0.976 and 0.954 for the condyle, and 0.966 
and 0.936 for the glenoid fossa, respectively. The present

slightly lower than those reported by Öztürk et al. [27].
While artificial intelligence has demonstrated notable 
success in segmenting anatomical structures, its perfor­
mance can vary significantly depending on several fac­
tors [42]. These include differences in training and testing 
datasets, variations in model hyperparameters, and the 
specific anatomical structures targeted for segmenta­
tion, all of which play a crucial role in determining the 
accuracy and reliability of AI models. To enhance gen­
eralizability and reliability, it is essential to standardize 
evaluation metrics, use diverse datasets, and fine-tune 
models for specific applications.
Although our study achieved a high IoU value (0.8941) 
for hyoid bone segmentation using nnU-Net v2, this met­
ric was slightly lower than those reported in studies by 
Öztürk et al. [27]. and Vinayahalingam et al. [38], which 
focused on larger and morphologically more distinct 
craniofacial structures. These differences may be attrib­
uted to the anatomical complexity and variability of the 
hyoid bone. Unlike the relatively stable shape and posi­
tion of the maxillary sinus or mandibular condyle, the 
hyoid bone is a small, mobile, and non-articulating struc­
ture influenced by various muscular attachments and 
functional movements. The lack of direct skeletal artic­
ulation and its positional variability—affected by head 
posture and surrounding soft tissue tension—can result 
in lower contrast boundaries on CBCT imaging, posing 
challenges for consistent automatic segmentation.
Furthermore, segmentation performance may be 
affected by heterogeneity in the training datasets. In our 
study, we included a relatively broad skeletal classification 
and range of anatomical variability, which may introduce 
additional complexity. In contrast, the referenced studies 
may have benefited from more homogeneous datasets or 
anatomically larger and easier-to-segment targets [27, 35, 
38].
Therefore, while our model demonstrated robust 
overall performance, the inherently more variable and 
anatomically complex nature of the hyoid bone may 
contribute to modest differences in performance met­
rics such as IoU when compared to other craniofacial 
structures.
On the other hand, comparing our results with those of 
similar CBCT-based segmentation studies highlights the 
significant role of anatomical complexity. Structures such 
as the bifid mandibular canal or the nasolacrimal canal, 
which are more difficult to isolate and segment from sur­
rounding tissues compared to the hyoid bone, have dem­
onstrated lower performance metrics in the literature.

For instance, in a study that applied the same nnU-Net 
v2 architecture to the anatomically complex yet relatively 
fixed nasolacrimal canal, an IoU of 0.7341 was reported 
[43]. Similarly, another study reported an IoU of approxi­
mately 0.701 for the larger and continuous mandibular 
canal, while the more variable bifid mandibular canal 
yielded a considerably lower IoU of around 0.332 [44]. 
These findings support the notion that anatomical size, 
shape variability, and contextual contrast heavily influ­
ence segmentation performance, even when utilizing the 
same deep learning architecture [45–47].
CBCT provides a reliable and accurate method for 
evaluating the cranio-maxillofacial structure, as well as 
the position and morphology of the hyoid bone. CBCT 
scans obtained prior to orthodontic diagnosis and treat­
ment allow for a clear clinical assessment of the upper 
airway space and the position of the hyoid bone. There­
fore, CBCT has become a widely adopted method for 
early diagnosis and evaluation. Assessing the upper air­
way with CBCT is an essential step before planning orth­
odontic or orthognathic surgery. However, CBCT scans 
are rarely used for an in-depth examination of the hyoid 
bone, indicating that the full potential of the technology 
is not being fully realized. Particularly, the effects of dif­
ferent skeletal malocclusions and abnormalities on the 
tongue and the hyoid bone play a critical role in treat­
ment planning. Through CBCT, more detailed and accu­
rate data regarding the position of the tongue and the 
hyoid bone in such patients can be obtained, allowing for 
a more effective treatment process [13, 48, 49].
Labeling the HB using artificial intelligence presents a 
significant innovation in this context. Traditional manual 
labeling is time-consuming and prone to errors, while 
AI-based systems automate this process, improving accu­
racy and accelerating clinical workflows. Deep learning 
algorithms can detect and label the hyoid bone on CBCT 
scans with high precision. For clinicians, especially in 
busy clinical environments with high patient loads and 
limited time, manual labeling can be quite challenging 
[21–24]. This approach is particularly beneficial for pro­
fessionals who may have difficulty identifying anatomi­
cal structures such as the HB. The use of such automated 
systems can assist in making faster and more reliable 
treatment planning and intervention decisions.
Moreover, the broader utility of artificial intelligence 
in biomedical imaging has been underscored in various 
domains. For instance, Ali et al. [50] demonstrated the 
applicability of deep learning, machine learning, and AI 
techniques in the automated analysis of microscopic cell 
and tissue images, enabling objective interpretation and 
reducing inter-observer variability in diagnostic pathol­
ogy. Although their study focused on microscopic image 
analysis, the underlying principles—standardization, 
reproducibility, and high-throughput processing—are 
equally relevant to macroscopic imaging modalities like 
CBCT. Our findings align with this perspective, illustrat­
ing how an AI-based segmentation framework such as 
nnU-Net v2 can be effectively employed to identify and 
delineate complex anatomical structures like the hyoid 
bone. This convergence of AI applications across imaging 
scales highlights its growing versatility and transforma­
tive impact in both diagnostic and therapeutic workflows.
Despite reaching significant findings, this study has 
several limitations: The CBCT images used in the study 
were obtained from a single center (Inönü University). 
This may limit the generalizability of the model to differ­
ent populations. The performance of the model against 
different ethnic backgrounds, age groups, and anatomi­
cal variations should be evaluated using a broader and 
more diverse dataset. Although the study discussed the 
potential clinical applications of HB segmentation, there 
was no direct test or validation of the model’s use in real 
clinical practice. The accuracy of the segmentation was 
assessed in the study, but further studies are needed to 
determine how the segmentation can be integrated into 
the clinical decision-making process.
Conclusions
The clinical significance of the HB is considerable across 
various medical and dental disciplines. As an attach­
ment site for muscles involved in essential functions 
such as mastication, swallowing, speech, and respiration, 
it plays a critical role in the functional orofacial system. 
In orthodontics and dentofacial orthopedics, the posi­
tion and mobility of the hyoid bone are directly related 
to the positioning of the mandible and tongue, making it 
an important reference point in the assessment of skel­
etal malocclusions. In the fields of otolaryngology and 
general surgery, the anatomical relationship of the HB 
with surrounding structures must be carefully evalu­
ated in procedures such as thyroidectomy, neck dis­
sections, and laryngeal surgeries to reduce the risk of 
complications. Moreover, a significant correlation has 
been found between the position of the HB and upper 
airway obstructions such as obstructive sleep apnea; a 
posteriorly or inferiorly positioned HB may contribute to 
airway narrowing. From a forensic medicine perspective, 
HB fractures can serve as an important diagnostic crite­
rion in cases of strangulation. For all these reasons, the 
anatomy and clinical implications of the HB should be 
approached through a multidisciplinary perspective. In 
this study, the nnU-Net v2 model successfully performed 
automated segmentation of the HB in CBCT images. This 
approach demonstrates promising accuracy and consis­
tency, and may support future integration into clinical 
workflows, pending further validation studies focused on 
efficiency and usability.

Abstract: Objective This study aimed to identify the hyoid bone (HB) using the nnU-Net based artificial intelligence (AI) model in cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) images and assess the model’s success in automatic segmentation. Methods CBCT images of 190 patients were randomly selected. The raw data was converted to DICOM format and transferred to the 3D Slicer Imaging Software (Version 4.10.2; MIT, Cambridge, MA, USA). HB was labeled manually using the 3D Slicer. The dataset was divided into training, validation, and test sets in a ratio of 8:1:1. The nnU-Net v2 architecture was utilized to process the training and test datasets, generating the algorithm weight factors. To assess the model’s accuracy and performance, a confusion matrix was employed. F1-score, Dice coefficient (DC), 95% Hausdorff distance (95% HD), and Intersection over Union (IoU) metrics were calculated to evaluate the results. Results The model’s performance metrics were as follows: DC = 0.9434, IoU = 0.8941, F1-score = 0.9446, and 95% HD = 1.9998. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was generated, yielding an AUC value of 0.98. Conclusion The results indicated that the nnU-Net v2 model achieved high precision and accuracy in HB segmentation on CBCT images. Automatic segmentation of HB can enhance clinicians’ decision-making speed and accuracy in diagnosing and treating various clinical conditions. Clinical trial number Not applicable.
